proves: align-items: baseline aligns three runs of different sizes on their baselines, and align-items: flex-start does not move.
checkable: 360x190, two rows of three runs at 14, 22 and 34 point, each run's first glyph an H whose ink bottom is its baseline. The three runs occupy x=16..41, 51..89 and 100..158 in both rows. Row 0 sets align-items:baseline: the three H bottoms are all 56, one y shared by all three. Row 1 is align-items:flex-start and the control: H bottoms 108, 117 and 132, which is what flex-start means. Read the H rather than the run: the runs carry descenders, so a run's lowest ink is below its baseline by an amount that grows with the font size, and comparing those would report three numbers that differ for a second reason.
chrome: measured in Chrome on the equivalent CSS, ink threshold 128, reading the FULL WORD's ink including descenders. Row 0 (align-items: baseline): tops 46, 39, 29 and bottoms 59, 60, 62 for 14px, 22px, 34px. Row 1 (align-items: flex-start, the control): tops 99, 101, 106 and bottoms 112, 122, 139.
against_chrome: row 0 full-word tops are 46, 39, 29 here, matching Chrome on all three. Bottoms are 59, 60, 63 against Chrome's 59, 60, 62 -- two exact and the 34pt one row low, which is the faintest antialiased row landing either side of the threshold and the same one-row difference the control row shows at 34pt.
the_sign_is_what_this_pins: Chrome's row 0 bottoms INCREASE with size -- 59, 60, 62 -- because aligned baselines let a larger descender hang further below the line. A renderer that aligns box bottoms instead produces a DECREASING run, because a shared bottom edge puts the small text's ink lowest. The trend is the discriminator, not the spread: an implementation that narrowed the gap while keeping the order inverted would pass a 'the baselines should be level' test and fail this one.
two_different_bottoms_live_in_this_scene: the word is Hxgp, so its full-word ink bottom is a descender and its leftmost glyph's bottom is the baseline. They are different numbers and only one is comparable with Chrome's: full-word 59, 60, 63 against Chrome's 59, 60, 62; leftmost-glyph 56, 56, 56, which is the reading that says the baselines are level.
measured: H has no descender, so its ink bottom IS the baseline. Row 0's three H-bottoms share one y; row 1 is align-items:flex-start and is expected to differ.
why_a_measured_leaf_is_the_case: a flex item with no baseline of its own aligns on its bottom margin edge, so a row of plain boxes gives the same answer under baseline and under flex-end and cannot tell the two rules apart. chrome_tables.rs's thirty-row flex matrix is exactly that: its children are spacer boxes, its baseline rows agree with Chrome, and they say nothing about this. Text is the only leaf whose baseline is measured rather than derived, which is what makes it the case that discriminates.
what_carries_the_baseline: layout.rs's measure closure builds taffy's LayoutOutput itself and sets baselines from MeasuredLeaf::first_baseline, offset by the leaf's own top padding and border because CSS measures a flex item's baseline from its border box. taffy reads a missing baseline as the node's height (taffy-0.14.0/src/compute/flexbox.rs:1921), which is the box-bottom rule this scene is built to tell apart from the real one.
grid: grid routes leaves through the same compute_leaf_layout, and taffy carries `TODO: Support baseline alignment in the vertical axis` at taffy-0.14.0/src/compute/grid/mod.rs:345 and :531. Extending this fixture to a grid would ask a question taffy does not answer.
status: both rows are measured against Chrome and match. Read the sign rather than the spread.
